tagline: Riverbank roads connect working farmland, covered bridges and old town centers.
intro: The Connecticut River Byway follows a corridor of roads on both sides of the river through Vermont and New Hampshire, with a Massachusetts section through farms and historic town centers. The National Scenic Byway Foundation lists a 2005 national designation and describes a landscape of floodplains, stepped terraces and upland slopes. In Massachusetts, the regional byway organization highlights rolling hills, forests, pastures and active farms growing crops that include apples and asparagus. On the New Hampshire bank, NH 12A winds through hilly terrain north of Charlestown.

Bridges changed travel between the banks. Colonel Enoch Hale built the first bridge across the Connecticut at Bellows Falls in 1785. At Cornish and Windsor, three earlier bridges preceded the covered crossing built in 1866. New Hampshire bought that bridge in 1936, but tolls remained until 1943.

For a circuit, take the Vermont corridor north through Bellows Falls, Windsor and St. Johnsbury. Farther north, VT 102 follows the west bank from Guildhall through Lemington to Canaan near the Canadian border. Columbia Bridge links VT 102 with US 3 across the river. On the New Hampshire return, pass Orford, Hanover and Claremont before continuing south toward the Massachusetts farm towns. Routes 63 and 47 carry the farm byway through Montague Center.
notice: In Massachusetts, family farms, forests, pastures and historic town centers line the byway.

moments.title: Cornish-Windsor Covered Bridge
moments.text: The Cornish-Windsor crossing charged different pedestrian tolls by direction when its present bridge opened in 1866. A 1966 New Hampshire Division of Economic Development report recalled two cents to enter “wet” Cornish and three cents to return to “dry” Windsor. Bela Jenks Fletcher and James Frederick Tasker built the present bridge in 1866. Its timber lattice follows a design patented by Ithiel Town. The two-span timber structure stretches approximately 449 feet across the river and is 24 feet wide. New Hampshire purchased the crossing in 1936 and removed the toll seven years later.

moments.title: Columbia Covered Bridge
moments.text: Columbia Bridge is the third crossing built on this site between Lemington, Vermont, and Columbia, New Hampshire. Charles Babbitt built it in 1912 after fire destroyed its predecessor the year before. The crossing carries Columbia Bridge Road between VT 102 and US 3 through a rural agricultural setting. Its single, 146-foot span uses a Howe truss of wood and iron. Vertical boards cover the exterior and continue a short way inside the entrances to protect the truss ends. On the north side, a gap remains between the siding and the gabled roof.
moments.notice: An open strip separates the north-side siding from the gabled roof.

moments.title: Orford
moments.text: Orford’s Seven Swans are a row of Federal-style houses on The Ridge, built between 1773 and 1839. The dwellings show the influence of architect Asher Benjamin. Down on the Connecticut in 1793, Samuel Morey demonstrated a paddlewheel propelling a steamboat. His interest in steam power followed work at his father’s ferry. Agriculture employed most residents by 1859, alongside mills, a tannery and factories making chairs, footwear and building components. The main village lies along NH 10 beside the river; the town hall is in Orfordville, several miles east of the river on NH 25A.
